Juvenile Japanese giant salamanders exhibit a remarkably slow growth trajectory during their early years. This rate of size increase continues at a measured pace, so that by the third year of life, individuals typically measure roughly 20 centimeters  in total bod at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]y length. Both of these early-life length measurements were recorded in wild populations under consistent thermal conditions of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], a temperature that dominates their subterranean and deep-pool microhabitats. The modest size achieved during these formative years stands in stark contrast to the truly gigantic proportions this species can attain over a long life span, and it underscores the importance of slow, steady somatic investment. Field surveys suggest that survival during this period is high, likely due to the aggressive territorial defense of nest sites by attending males, which protects the yolk-sac larvae and later the exogenously feeding tadpoles from predation.

Upon hatching from the gelatinous egg mass, the neonate or yolk-dependent larva emerges at a very small size, with a total length at birth of merely 3 centimeters [Lb = 3 centimeters]. This diminutive initial length, measured across numerous clutches in the wild, represents the starting point for the substantial growth required to reach the species' impressive adult dimensions. Development proceeds through a prolonged larval phase, during which the gill-breathing tadpole gradually increases in mass. Remarkably, an individual measuring 136 centimeters in total body length, which is already considered a very large adult, has a corresponding wet weight of 26,300 grams (26300 grams) . This weight-to-length relationship provides a useful reference point for assessing body condition in wild populations and highlights the substantial tissue mass that accumulates slowly over many decades of life. The maximum or ultimate wet weight recorded for this species is 36,000 grams (36000 grams) [Wwi = 36000 grams], a value that places Andrias japonicus among the heaviest of all extant amphibians and reflects its ability to exploit a protein-rich diet of fish, crustaceans, and frogs within its cool, stable environment.

The ultimate total length recorded for the Japanese giant salamander is 150 centimeters [Li = 150 centimeters], a remarkable size that is complemented by a snout-to-vent length of 90 centimeters in the largest specimens examined. This ultimate size is not reached until very late in life, consistent with the species' extremely slow growth trajectory and extended longevity. In stark contrast to these enormous adults, the onset of reproductive maturity occurs at a much more modest body size. The average total length at puberty is 35 centimeters [Lp = 35 centimeters], although there is a clear sexual dimorphism: males typically mature when they reach a total length of 30 centimeters, while females do not attain sexual maturation until they have grown to approximately 40 centimeters in total length. This size-based divergence in maturation thresholds is a common pattern among amphibians and likely reflects the greater energetic demands of egg production in females. Observational data indicate that once these size thresholds are crossed, individuals begin to participate in the communal breeding aggregations that are a hallmark of their reproductive biology.

Under the stable, cool thermal conditions of their montane stream habitats, where water temperature averages approximately 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the Japanese giant salamander completes its embryonic development within a period of about 50 days [ab = about 50 days]. This incubation period, measured from the moment of external fertilisation during amplexus to the hatching event, is relatively prolonged compared to many temperate-zone amphibians, a consequence of the low metabolic rates imposed by the cold environment. Following this extended incubation, the larvae emerge as endotrophic, yolk-dependent tadpoles that remain in the egg chamber guarded by the male for several weeks until the onset of exogenous feeding. The total lifespan of this species is exceptionally long, with the maximum recorded longevity in the wild estimated at 80 years [am = 80 years] at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This extraordinary lifespan, among the greatest for any amphibian, is linked directly to the species' slow metabolic pace and the low predation pressure within its deep, rocky refuges. Comparative studies of giant salamanders in the family Cryptobranchidae suggest that such extended longevity, coupled with delayed maturity, represents an evolutionary strategy adapted to stable, food-limited environments where adult survival is paramount.

Sexual maturity, as measured by the capacity to participate in annual spawning aggregations, is not achieved until an individual is quite advanced in age. Under the typical thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the age at first reproduction is 15 years after birth [tR = 15 years after birth]. This remarkably delayed onset of breeding is among the latest recorded for any amphibian and reflects the substantial time required for an individual to accumulate the body mass necessary to compete for prime nesting sites within the stream bed. The maximum reproductive rate, or annual egg output of a single large female under optimal conditions, is equally impressive, with a single female depositing a single large string of approximately 1,000 eggs annually [Ri = approximately 1,000 eggs annually]. The combination of extreme longevity, very late first reproduction, and high fecundity per event defines a life-history strategy that is highly sensitive to the removal of large, old individuals from the breeding population.
